To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the membrane transport changes seen in transformed and density-inhibited cells were not seen in cells as they traversed the cell cycle and 2) the membrane transport and morphological changes were not related to one another.
cell surface changes associated both with growth control and with malignant transformation are not linked to the cell division cycle.

the changes in membrane function that are characteristic of density-inhibition and malignant transformation do not appear in normal cells as they traverse their cell cycles, and that the expression of tumor virus genes can cause a transformation-specific change at any stage in normal cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the cell cycle in the control of membrane function and with the mechanism by which tumor virus genes alter cell membrane function.
the relationship of cell surface changes to cell growth and to the expression of viral oncogenes.
the role that cell membrane function may play in growth control and malignant conversion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the membrane changes seen in density-inhibited cells and in cells transformed by tumor virus gene expression are not linked to the cell-cycle phase in which they occur, and they do not appear to be linked to each other.

the membrane changes associated with density inhibition or transformation are not cell cycle dependent, nor is the expression of the tumor virus gene product dependent on progression through the cell division cycle.
cell surface alterations are not linked to the cell division cycle and that the expression of tumor virus genes is independent of cell cycle progression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cell cycle is an important determinant of membrane function in normal cells, but that the cell cycle does not appear to be involved in the expression of tumor virus genes.
the changes in membrane function characteristic of growth control and malignant transformed cells are not directly linked to the cell division cycle.

the changes in membrane function associated with growth control or malignant transformation do not appear to be directly coupled to the cell cycle, although they may be coupled to the cell division cycle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are no obvious cell cycle-dependent changes of membrane function that are correlated with the changes in growth control or with malignant transformation.

the cell surface changes associated either with growth control or with malignant transformation can occur at any stage in cell cycle progression and do not necessarily require progression through the cell division cycle.
the cell surface changes seen in transformed cells are not a consequence of the malignant transformation but rather a consequence of the expression of viral genes in the transformed cell.
